copy.bottomLine: Output per hour is pulling further above its old trend: 2.5% a year since the end of 2023, against 1.6% in 2004–19. That is closer to a reliable signal, but chance alone could still produce a gap this large about 10% of the time. The main holdout is underlying efficiency: the San Francisco Fed finds almost no gain, and credits the extra output to more machines and people working harder. The verdict would move if the pickup holds for another quarter or two and underlying efficiency starts rising with it.
copy.changed: Latest releases: Q3 Productivity and Costs (BLS, Nov 5) put nonfarm output per hour up at a 3.6% annual rate in Q3 and revised earlier quarters up, lifting the pace since the end of 2023 from 2.1% to 2.5% a year. The chance that noise explains it fell from 22% to 10%, still short of the 5% bar, so the verdict stays at Not yet.

caseFor.h: The pickup is broad and getting stronger.
caseFor.body: Output per hour has grown 2.5% a year since the end of 2023 on both the nonfarm business and nonfinancial corporate measures, against 1.6% and 1.4% in 2004–19. Q3 alone ran at a 3.6% annual rate. Official BLS TFP has grown 1.2% a year since 2023, against 0.7%, and real income outpaces real GDP.

caseFor.h: Where AI is built, productivity is surging.
caseFor.body: Output per hour in information has grown 9.9% a year since the end of 2023, against 6.0% in 2010–19: output up 8.2% a year while hours fell 1.5%. That speed-up is larger than in any 2010–19 stretch.
Professional and business services have sped up 1.8 points more than retail, leisure and construction, each against its own 2010–19 pace. A year ago the gap was 0.3 points.

The SF Fed credits the gains to working harder, a signal Klein finds comes almost entirely from manufacturing workweeks. Longer shifts at machine shops say little about whether coders and analysts are getting more done.

Output per hour only took off around 1997, years after tech stocks were priced for a boom. Inflation-adjusted investment in computers and related equipment is up 55.9% in two years, and payoffs from new technology usually come after firms reorganize.

caseAgainst.body: Strip out more machines, more skills and harder work, and the SF Fed's figures show underlying efficiency growing about 0.1% a year since the end of 2023, essentially flat. In the 1997–2003 boom it grew about 2.1% a year.

caseAgainst.h: The headline pace is still within normal noise.
caseAgainst.body: Chance alone would put nonfarm output per hour this far above trend about 10% of the time; a reliable signal needs 5% or less. Eleven quarters in, it is up 6.9%, against 9.1% at the same point in the 1990s, and every stretch of that boom was faster.

caseAgainst.h: More machines and longer hours explain a lot.
caseAgainst.body: In the SF Fed's Q2 2026 figures, more capital and skills per hour added 1.7 points to 2.3% labor-productivity growth and working harder added another 1.7, while efficiency subtracted 1.1. Factory production workers average 42.0 hours a week, up 1.2 in two years.

Retail's 2.0-point slowdown supplies much of the office-versus-hands-on gap; drop any one hands-on industry and it shrinks to 1.1 points. Some 2010–19 stretches showed gaps as large. Information's surge reflects building and selling AI, not using it.

This week's revisions lifted the nonfarm figures but cut nonfinancial corporations from 2.7% to 2.5% a year since the end of 2023. Early estimates move a lot, and the corporate figure for Q3 isn't out until December.
